claim: Regional NAT gateways were introduced on November 19, 2025: one NAT gateway that automatically expands across Availability Zones based on your workload footprint, instead of one zonal NAT gateway per Availability Zone.
question: When did regional NAT gateways launch, and what changed compared with zonal NAT gateways?

values.spoken: November nineteenth, twenty twenty-five

values.display: automatically expand across Availability Zones based on your workload footprint
values.spoken: expands across Availability Zones on its own as the workload grows

evidence.quote: | [Regional NAT gateways for automatic multi-AZ expansion](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateways-regional.html) | You can now use regional NAT gateways that automatically expand across Availability Zones based on your workload footprint. Regional NAT gateways provide simplified setup, enhanced security, and automatic high availability without manual intervention. | November 19, 2025 |
Unlike standard NAT gateways (referred to as zonal NAT gateways), which operate in a single Availability Zone, regional NAT gateways follow your workloads to provide automatic high availability.

With this launch, you can create a single NAT Gateway that automatically expands and contracts across availability zones (AZs) in your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) based on your workload presence, to maintain high availability while offering simplified setup and management.

note: FRESHNESS hypothesis confirmed. Older questions assume 'HA NAT means one NAT gateway per AZ in a public subnet'. GA 2025-11-19: examinable.

claim: A regional NAT gateway is a standalone resource with its own route table; you do not need a public subnet in your VPC to host it.
question: Does a regional NAT gateway need a public subnet?

values.display: do not need a public subnet
values.spoken: no public subnet needed

evidence.quote: A regional NAT Gateway is a standalone resource with its own route table and you do not need a public subnet in your VPC to host a regional NAT Gateway, which reduces chances of misconfiguring private resources in subnets with public connectivity.
You do not need a public subnet to host a regional NAT Gateway.

note: Contrast with a zonal public NAT gateway, which is created in a public subnet.

claim: A regional NAT gateway supports up to 32 IP addresses per Availability Zone, compared with 8 for a zonal NAT gateway; each IP address adds 55,000 concurrent connections to one destination.
question: How many IP addresses per Availability Zone does a regional NAT gateway support, compared with a zonal NAT gateway?

values.spoken: thirty-two IP addresses per Availability Zone
eight for a zonal NAT gateway
fifty-five thousand connections per IP address

qualifiers.scope: per regional NAT gateway, per Availability Zone

evidence.quote: Your regional NAT Gateways support up to 32 IP addresses per Availability Zone (compared to 8 for zonal NAT gateways). Each IP address increases the limit on concurrent connections to a popular destination (identified by unique combination of destination IP, destination port and protocol) by 55,000.

claim: A regional NAT gateway can take up to 60 minutes to expand to a new Availability Zone after a resource appears there; until then that traffic is handled across zones by the gateway in an existing Availability Zone.
question: How long can a regional NAT gateway take to expand to a new Availability Zone?

values.spoken: up to sixty minutes

evidence.quote: It may take your regional NAT Gateway up to 60 minutes to expand to a new Availability Zone after a resource is instantiated there. Until this expansion is complete, the relevant traffic from this resource is processed across zones by your regional NAT Gateway in one of the existing Availability Zones.

claim: Regional NAT gateways do not support private NAT and are not supported in constrained Availability Zones; for private NAT use a zonal NAT gateway.
question: Can a regional NAT gateway be used for private NAT?

values.spoken: no private NAT; use a zonal NAT gateway for that

evidence.quote: Regional NAT gateways do not support private NAT. If you need private NAT, use zonal NAT gateways instead. Regional NAT gateways are not supported in constrained Availability Zones.
Regional NAT Gateways do not offer private connectivity and we recommend using your NAT Gateways in zonal availability mode for private NAT use cases.

claim: A regional NAT gateway runs in automatic mode, where AWS manages the IP addresses and the Availability Zone expansion, or in manual mode, where you manage the IP addresses and expand and contract the gateway across Availability Zones yourself.
question: What are the automatic and manual modes of a regional NAT gateway?

values.display: AWS automatically manages IP addresses and Availability Zone expansion
values.spoken: automatic mode: AWS manages addresses and zone expansion

values.display: you are responsible for expanding and contracting your NAT gateway across Availability Zones
values.spoken: manual mode: you expand and contract it yourself

evidence.quote: In this mode, AWS automatically manages IP addresses and Availability Zone expansion (recommended).
In manual mode, you are responsible for expanding and contracting your NAT gateway across Availability Zones.

claim: A regional NAT gateway is charged one NAT Gateway-hour for every Availability Zone it is configured in, plus the data processing charge per gigabyte; when it leaves an Availability Zone the charge for that zone stops.
question: How is a regional NAT gateway billed?

values.display: charged for each hour that the NAT Gateway is configured in each availability zone
values.spoken: one gateway-hour per Availability Zone it runs in

qualifiers.scope: per regional NAT gateway, per Availability Zone

evidence.quote: If you choose to create a NAT gateway with regional availability in your VPC, you are charged for each hour that the NAT Gateway is configured in each availability zone. For example, if your regional NAT is running across three Availability Zones(AZs) for one hour, you'll be billed for three 'NAT Gateway-hours'. When your regional NAT removes support from an AZ following changes in your workload footprint, billing automatically adjusts - you'll stop incurring charges for that specific AZ. Data processing charges apply for each gigabyte processed through the NAT gateway regardless of the traffic's source or destination.

note: Cost dimension; the per-hour rate itself is on the pricing page ($0.045 per hour per AZ in US East (Ohio) in the example) and belongs to the numbers lens.

claim: A NAT gateway supports 5 Gbps of bandwidth and automatically scales up to 100 Gbps; since June 15, 2022 the ceiling is 100 Gbps, up from 45 Gbps. If you need more, split resources into several subnets with a NAT gateway each.
question: How much bandwidth does a NAT gateway support, and what was the previous maximum?

values.spoken: five gigabits per second
up to one hundred gigabits per second
forty-five gigabits per second (old value)

qualifiers.condition: automatic scaling; split subnets for more

evidence.quote: A NAT gateway supports 5 Gbps of bandwidth and automatically scales up to 100 Gbps. If you require more bandwidth, you can split your resources into multiple subnets and create a NAT gateway in each subnet.

| [NAT gateway bandwidth](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html#nat-gateway-basics) | NAT gateways now support bandwidth up to 100 Gbps (an increase from 45 Gbps) and can process up to 10 million packets per second (up from four million packets). | June 15, 2022 |

note: Older material says 45 Gbps; the history row dates the change to June 15, 2022, a few weeks before the book's change window.

claim: A NAT gateway processes 1 million packets per second and automatically scales up to 10 million packets per second; beyond that it drops packets. Since June 15, 2022 the ceiling is 10 million, up from 4 million packets per second.
question: How many packets per second can a NAT gateway process?

values.display: up to 10 million packets per second
values.spoken: up to ten million packets per second
one million packets per second to start

evidence.quote: A NAT gateway can process one million packets per second and automatically scales up to 10 million packets per second. Beyond this limit, a NAT gateway will drop packets. To prevent packet loss, split your resources into multiple subnets and create a separate NAT gateway for each subnet.

| [NAT gateway bandwidth](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html#nat-gateway-basics) | NAT gateways now support bandwidth up to 100 Gbps (an increase from 45 Gbps) and can process up to 10 million packets per second (up from four million packets). | June 15, 2022 |

claim: NAT gateways support an MTU of 8500 (documented September 10, 2024); packets larger than 8500 bytes are dropped or fragmented, and instances that reach the internet through a public NAT gateway should keep their MTU at 1500 bytes or less.
question: What MTU does a NAT gateway support, and what MTU should instances behind a public NAT gateway use?

values.spoken: eighty-five hundred bytes
keep the instance MTU at fifteen hundred bytes for internet traffic

evidence.quote: Packets larger than 8500 bytes that arrive at the NAT gateway are dropped (or fragmented, if applicable).
To prevent potential packet loss when communicating with resources over the internet using a public NAT gateway, the MTU setting for your EC2 instances should not exceed 1500 bytes.

| [NAT gateway MTU support](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateway-basics.html) | NAT gateways support traffic with a maximum transmission unit (MTU) of 8500. | September 10, 2024 |

claim: Each IPv4 address on a NAT gateway supports up to 55,000 simultaneous connections to each unique destination (destination IP, destination port and protocol); you can raise the limit by associating up to 8 IPv4 addresses (1 primary and 7 secondary) with the NAT gateway.
question: How many simultaneous connections to one destination does a NAT gateway support per IP address, and how is the limit raised?

values.spoken: fifty-five thousand simultaneous connections per IP address
up to eight IPv4 addresses, one primary and seven secondary

qualifiers.scope: per NAT gateway IPv4 address, per unique destination
qualifiers.condition: raise by adding secondary IPv4 addresses

evidence.quote: Each IPv4 address can support up to 55,000 simultaneous connections to each unique destination. A unique destination is identified by a unique combination of destination IP address, the destination port, and protocol (TCP/UDP/ICMP). You can increase this limit by associating up to 8 IPv4 addresses to your NAT gateways (1 primary IPv4 address and 7 secondary IPv4 addresses).

| [Add secondary IPv4 addresses to NAT gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html#nat-gateway-edit-secondary) | You can add secondary private IPv4 addresses to public and private NAT gateways. Secondary IPv4 addresses increase the number of available ports, and therefore they increase the limit on the number of concurrent connections that your workloads can establish using a NAT gateway. | January 31, 2023 |

note: Secondary IPv4 addresses on NAT gateways arrived January 31, 2023; older material knows only the 55,000 per gateway figure.

claim: Since January 31, 2023 you can add secondary private IPv4 addresses to public and private NAT gateways; they add ports and so raise the number of concurrent connections the gateway can hold.
question: When did NAT gateways gain secondary private IPv4 addresses, and why add them?

values.spoken: January thirty-first, twenty twenty-three

values.display: increase the number of available ports
values.spoken: more ports, so more concurrent connections

evidence.quote: | [Add secondary IPv4 addresses to NAT gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html#nat-gateway-edit-secondary) | You can add secondary private IPv4 addresses to public and private NAT gateways. Secondary IPv4 addresses increase the number of available ports, and therefore they increase the limit on the number of concurrent connections that your workloads can establish using a NAT gateway. | January 31, 2023 |

Secondary IPv4 addresses are optional and should be assigned or allocated when your workloads that use a NAT gateway exceed 55,000 concurrent connections to a single destination (the same destination IP, destination port, and protocol).

claim: A public NAT gateway can have 2 Elastic IP addresses associated by default; you raise this with a quota increase.
question: How many Elastic IP addresses can a public NAT gateway have by default?

values.spoken: two Elastic IP addresses by default

evidence.quote: You are limited to associating 2 Elastic IP addresses to your public NAT gateway by default. You can increase this limit by requesting a quota adjustment.

note: The quota table row 'Elastic IP addresses per public NAT gateway' (up to 8) belongs to the numbers lens.

claim: Since November 17, 2022 you can pick the primary private IPv4 address of a NAT gateway when you create it; previously the address was assigned automatically from the subnet range. You cannot change or remove it later, but you can add secondary private IPv4 addresses.
question: Can you choose the private IP address of a NAT gateway, and since when?

values.spoken: November seventeenth, twenty twenty-two

values.display: can't change or remove the primary private IPv4 address
values.spoken: the primary private address cannot be changed later

evidence.quote: | [Pick the private IP address of your NAT gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html#nat-gateway-creating) | When you create a NAT gateway, you can now choose to pick the private IP address that's assigned to the NAT gateway. Previously, the private IP address was automatically assigned from the IP address range of the subnet. | November 17, 2022 |

When you create a NAT gateway, you can select the primary private IPv4 address to assign to the NAT gateway. Otherwise, we select one on your behalf from the the IPv4 address range of the subnet. You can't change or remove the primary private IPv4 address. You can add secondary private IPv4 addresses as needed.

changed.was: the private IP address was automatically assigned from the IP address range of the subnet

claim: Since February 1, 2024 AWS charges $0.005 per IP per hour for every public IPv4 address, in use or idle, including the public IPv4 addresses of running instances and Elastic IP addresses; before that date an in-use public IPv4 address had no charge.
question: Are public IPv4 addresses and attached Elastic IP addresses charged, how much, and since when?

values.spoken: half a cent per address per hour
February first, twenty twenty-four

values.display: AWS charges for all public IPv4 addresses
values.spoken: every public IPv4 address is billed, attached or not

qualifiers.scope: per public IPv4 address, all AWS services and Regions

evidence.quote: Effective February 1, 2024 there will be a charge of $0.005 per IP per hour for all public IPv4 addresses, whether attached to a service or not (there is already a charge for public IPv4 addresses you allocate in your account but don’t attach to an EC2 instance).

| In-use Public IPv4 address (including Amazon provided public IPv4 and Elastic IP) assigned to resources in your VPC, Amazon Global Accelerator, and AWS Site-to-site VPN tunnel | No charge | $0.005 |
evidence.table_header: | Public IP Address Type | Current Price/Hour (USD) | New Price/Hour (USD) (Effective February 1, 2024) |

evidence.quote: AWS charges for all public IPv4 addresses, including public IPv4 addresses associated with running instances and Elastic IP addresses.

The price is the same whether the public IPv4 address is in-use public IPv4 addresses that is associated with an AWS resource you own, or an idle public IPv4 addresses in your AWS account not associated with any AWS resources.

note: FRESHNESS hypothesis confirmed: 'an attached Elastic IP is free' is wrong since 2024-02-01. Cost answers now favor IPv6, or a NAT gateway or load balancer front end over one public IP per instance.
